This study develops a novel, data-driven time series modeling approach, which we've called the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariites (TV-PARX). Unlike many existing models, TV-PARX is capable of capturing nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks through its dynamic parameters. Additionally, this model differs from traditional count series models by incorporating an underlying process that is Poisson-distributed, allowing for zero inflations and undercounts to be represented. We've also developed an efficient, Bayesian inference method to analyze TV-PARX, which involves a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm with a series of tailored moves to accurately estimate its dynamic parameters. This TV-PARX model can be applied to various time-varying data analysis tasks, including forecasting future values, identifying structural breaks, and analyzing nonlinear dynamics. Moreover, to evaluate the performance of TV-PARX, we conducted a series of simulation experiments that demonstrated its advantages over existing models.

To determine vertical aerosol optical depth without absolute calibration, we combined wide-field photometry from a network of telescopes observing the same field. This method relies on relative calibration, derived from the same frame's stellar and background regions. By applying this technique to multiple fields captured by the ATLAS telescope, we measured the vertical aerosol optical depth (VD) during the 2019-2020 Australian bushfire season. Compared to a reference site with known VD, we determined the relative VD of other sites, which showed good agreement with collocated OSIRIS spectrometer data. We also observed a positive correlation between VD and dust emission in the Magellan museum data from 2016-2019.

Numerous numerical methods are available for simulating complex biomolecular systems, and in this work, we examine the methods' performance when describing the behavior of the alanine dipeptide system. By using highly accurate reference solutions as benchmarks, we assess the accuracy and efficiency of Ab initio, DFT, and post-Hartree-Fock theories, as well as the effectiveness of describing active space through bond pair inversion. Our results show that in certain configurations, certain methods yield significantly inaccurate descriptions of the system's geometry, despite delivering comparable energies. This findings suggest that both accuracy and flexibility are crucial factors in choosing a simulation approach. Furthermore, we investigate the computational costs and advantages of employing medium-sized active spaces in conjunction with near-exact correlation treatments, as opposed to larger active spaces with tighter thresholds.

Human-generated descriptions of images are highly effective in conveying their content to visually impaired users but are time-consuming and costly to produce.  Due to their effectiveness, there's been interest in using artificial intelligence to generate image descriptions, with early approaches utilizing attributes and semantic segmentation and later approaches using fully convolution neural networks and their variants.  However, these methods are prone to errors and inaccuracies, which can lead to confusing descriptions and disappoint visually impaired users.  To improve the quality of automatically generated image descriptions, there's a growing need for better guidelines that balance creativity and accuracy, which is particularly important for users with visual impairments.  This paper introduces a new framework called Description Generation Evaluation Toolkit, which includes a set of guidelines and evaluation metrics to assist developers in creating more effective description generation models.  The authors conduct experiments using two datasets, FGVC and NII, and demonstrate the effectiveness of their framework by achieving higher description quality scores than previous methods, which leads to better performance in image classification tasks.  The results show that strict evaluation guidelines are essential in developing description generation models, which can be applied to a wide range of tasks, not just description generation, and and are particularly useful for visually impaired users with high visual abilities.

We establish a connection between Euler-Arnold equations and an optimization problem in quantum field theory, specifically for a class of Lagrangians known as "Hitchcock compatible." This involves using Madden-Ryan's previous work, as well as a toolbox of sophisticated mathematical techniques, including the Euler-Arnold equation's infinite-dimensional manifold representation, the theory of regular Euler-Arnold equations, and the Lagrange multipler rule in its infinite-dimensional form.

The interaction of heavy quarks is a key area of interest in QCD, particularly
for studying phenomena involving heavy flavor particles, such as charm and
beauty quarks. Despite the limited number of heavy flavors, multiple studies
have shown that new heavy quark flavors may be a possibility within certain
theoretical frameworks. One such model is the extended Standard Model with an
additional heavy flavor, which we refer to as "newness" (N). A previous study
conducting an analysis of data from proton-proton collisions found evidence of
a heavy scalar quark particle with a mass of approximately 1 TeV. To further
investigate this discovery, we performed a thorough analysis of the phenomenology
associated with heavy quark flavors, which serves as the foundation for our
search. A novel analysis approach was developed to identify the heavy scalar
quark particle through its decay products, which could potentially form bound
states with light quarks similar to charm quarks. This research marks the first
effort to create search strategies for heavy quark flavors that could potentially
form composite particles with light quarks. These strategies were employed to
conduct an inquiry into the presence of a heavy vector quark particle with a
mass of approximately 1 TeV by analyzing data from proton-proton collisions.

This research develops a method for solving a throughput optimization problem in wideband waveforming, which involves fair-throughput and total-throughput. Unlike narrowband approaches, this wideband strategy allows for the optimization of multiple user groups. The problem is framed as a bileterate linear program, which can be solved in polynomial time for small-scale networks. For larger networks, an iterative algorithm is developed, which converges quickly due to the tight approximation provided by a Lagrange multiplier.

Determining parton distribution functions is a challenging task, especially when fitting them to various data sets with significantly differing energy scales. While the DGLAP evolution equation accounts for PDF evolution, its accuracy is uncertain at very low scales. A new approach has been introduced, combining DGLAP evolution with NLO DGLAP initial state radiation, which significantly improves fit stability and reduces PDF errors. Using this method, we fitted the NNPDF40 dataset, resulting in the newly created NNPDF40s PDF set. Quark mass evolution was also incorporated to accurately determine strange PDFs. The NNPDF40s set exhibits improved description of data, particularly for low-x scattering experiments and anomalous magnetic moments of leptons.

This research focuses on a detailed analysis of a particular region of a turbulent reactive flow, utilizing the linearized framework, and investigates why one combustion model performs better than another when analyzing certain phenomena. A linearized framework is utilized to analyze a variable and a constant density model, as well as an equilibrium model, and the resulting equations are found to have similar physical interpretations. By comparing these models, we determine that a linearized equilibrium model closely resembles a linearized variable and a constant density model. Additionally, we utilize the linearized equilibrium model to investigate the influence of turbulence on chemical reactions and find that it leads to the same condition for reaction induction as the linearized variable and a constant density model.

We introduce a new choice of constitutive relation in nonlocal gravity theory, which differs from an previously established relation by an arbitrary constant. This constant, similar to other parameters in nonlocal gravity models, is considered a fundamental aspect of the theory, and its value can be determined through observable quantities. The nonlocality in the new model is analyzed and compared with the previous model, and both models are tested using moon data from the Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) technique. The results show that the new relation leads to a more concise framework with fewer parameters, and both the new and previous models produce comparable outcomes for the moon data.

A multidimensional analysis of multiparticle correlations in proton-proton collisions at the center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV is presented. Transverse momentum and centrality dependent correlations are examined for pions, kaons, and protons, focusing on the transverse recoil of the trigger particle. A significant side-by-side transverse momentum correlation is observed for protons and identified baryons in relation to mesons, indicating transverse flow that is not directly accessible through average transverse momenta. This information allows for a more precise determination of transverse flow, its impact on particle scattering phase space, and consequently, the structure of transverse phase space in proton-proton collisions.

This study explores the connection between neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) and the population of millisecond radio pulsars within the Galaxy. A key aspect of this research is the prediction of the number of LMXBs that should contain a millisecond neutron star, based on known formation theories and the observed population of binary systems. To conduct this analysis, we compiled a comprehensive list of all LMXBs within the Galaxy, taking into account both the known and unknown populations. Furthermore, we utilized observational data regarding the presence of millisecond pulsars in LMXBs, as well as information about the detection rates of pulsars and their binary companions. Utilizing the binary completion timescale, we calculated the overall population of LMXBs containing a millisecond neutron star, which is estimated to be approximately 50 systems. Additionally, we determined that at least 20 of these systems should exhibit millisecond pulsar behavior, although not all have been discovered yet.

We present a new method for creating planar drawings of bipartite graphs, which involves splitting selected vertices into triples while maintaining connectivity. This approach differs from previous similar methods, and we use it to solve the problem of finding the minimum number of vertex splittings required to create a planar drawing of a given bipartite graph.

HyperDegrade is a novel technique that enhances the effectiveness of side-channel attacks, specifically Flush+Reload attacks, by leveraging hyperparameters. This technique builds upon the previous LeakPrime approach and significantly improves the efficacy of these attacks in the context of both symmetric and asymmetric cryptography. HyperDegrade achieves this improved efficacy with lower amounts of side-channel information and with fewer traces required, demonstrating its effectiveness with 128-bit AES keys and demonstrating a feasibility study for a real-world protocol, the TLS handshake protocol. This protocol is critical for secure data transfer on the internet and hyperdegrading its side-channel properties through the use of HyperDegrade is key to exploiting its vulnerabilities to various attacks, including collision attacks, differential cryptanalysis, and generic attacks.

This research focuses on a type of operation called a diagonal move, specifically the local modification known as a delta move, which is relevant to certain types of knotted structures called rational tangles and catenanes. We present a study on the relationship between delta moves and the more commonly used switch moves, as well as the cross-over move, by analyzing their applicability to structures consisting of multiple connected components. Additionally, we examine the connection between delta moves and other types of adjustments, including the gamma move, the epsilon move, the sigma move, the tau move, the cross-over move, the switch move, and the gamma-cross move. A key contribution of this research involves developing a graphical representation of delta moves, thereby enabling their integration into software tools used for knot theory analysis, such as KnotPlot.

In collaborative systems where tasks are shared among agents, effective decision-making is crucial to complete tasks efficiently.  This is particularly true when agents can take on tasks of varying difficulty levels.  Previous work has focused on optimizing the choice of tasks based on their characteristics, but it has not explored how the distribution of task difficulties influences decision-making strategies.  This research fills this gap by investigating how the distribution of task difficulties affects the performance of both greedy and linear decision-making approaches in such systems.  Through comprehensive simulations, this study demonstrated that the performance of both approaches can be optimized by adjusting the difficulty distribution of available tasks.  Notably, this optimization leads to similar performance outcomes for both greedy and linear strategies, indicating that there is an optimal distribution where either approach can be effective.  This research also developed a novel linear decision-making method called 'Proportional' and compared it with existing methods, revealing that the 'Proportional' approach consistently delivers the best results across various distribution scenarios.  These findings provide valuable insights for designing efficient task management systems, especially those utilizing linear decision-making, by prescribing an optimal distribution of task difficulties, which can be applied to both single-agent and multi-agent scenarios.

We introduce the concept of a Cartesian Decomposition in the context of category theory, specifically for regular actions between groups and their resulting products. A Cartesian Decomposition is characterized by its interaction with the category's structure, particularly in relation to products, subgroups, and normal closure. We demonstrate that actions resulting in products with Cartesian Decomposition through a sequence of regular group actions are equivalent to actions facilitated by diagonal groups within the product's structure.

Building upon our previous work, we've developed a novel optical interferometer design called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, which offers enhanced sensitivity by exploiting optical wavefront manipulation and counter-intuitive signal processing. By utilizing two interconnected Sagnac interferometers in series, this design overcomes the traditional limit of quarter-wavelength displacement sensitivity, allowing for the detection of minute changes in distance. Notably, this design enables the measurement of wave-like, sloshing optical signals even when they're phase-shifted beyond recognition, thereby enabling the detection of disturbances as small as a few angstroms. This breakthrough results means that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer outperforms existing optical interferometer designs, opening up new possibilities for applications in gravitational physics, seismology, and interferometric sensing technology.

5G new radio extreme large scale multiple input multiple output (XL-MIMO) systems face significant random access (RA) challenges due to massive connectivity and limited resource pooling. To address this, we propose a new, priority-based RA protocol called NOVR-XL, which incorporates a new, efficient design called an embedded lattice ring (ELR) and a streamlined, priority-based search approach called XL-List. Furthermore, we develop a machine learning model called an extra-large scale neural network (XL-NN) to aid in ELR construction. Through comprehensive evaluations, NOVR-XL demonstrates substantial improvements over current standards, resulting in 2.5 times faster connection establishment, 30% reduced message lengths, and significant energy savings of up to 90%.

Neural language models have been highly effective in language tasks but are costly to train and use. On the other hand, $N$-gram models are more budget-friendly but less accurate. We present a new neural model called Neural Gram Models that combines the strengths of both, allowing for the reinforcement learning of both neural and $N$-gram models. This combination is particularly effective when the reinforcement learning is focused on tasks that are hard to perform with certain word contexts, such as translating rare words. We further developed an efficient way to train Neural Gram Models on large datasets by splitting the data into multiple parts. Our research resulted in the creation of three large neural language models: Chinea (1.2 terabytes), America (1.3 terabytes), and Europe (1.0 terabytes) that were used to conduct quality-assessment experiments on machine translation and summarization. Our findings showed significant improvements in performance compared to traditional neural models, and we also found that the performance of Neural Gram Models could be further enhanced by incorporating existing dictionary information.

The integration of advanced optical character recognition (OCR) systems and vote tabulation systems remains compromised due to OCR's inaccuracy. To address this, we developed a spell correction module that can be used to improve the accuracy of OCR in vote tabulation systems. Our approach utilizes a deep learning model to correct spelling errors from OCR output, and we conduct experiments on spell-checkable fonts that meet voting standards. The results show that our spell correction algorithm achieves the best performance compared to other methods, with an overall character accuracy of 99.5%. Additionally, we analyze the impact of font styles and sizes on OCR accuracy, and the data available for training the spell correction model is found to be highly effective.

A global atmospheric model has been used to investigate the formation of wave systems similar to baroclinic storms on Mars, as well as the resulting circulation patterns, which show similarities to those observed in an Earth-like atmosphere. Unlike Earth, Mars exhibits cold polar caps and strong temperature differences between the poles and the equator, leading to significant atmospheric wave activity and the formation of storm systems in the mid-latitudes. To better understand these storms, we utilized an global atmospheric model to study the development of wave systems similar to baroclinic storms on Mars, as well as the resulting circulation patterns, which reveal striking similarities to those observed in an Earth-like atmosphere. The results indicate that the formation of these storm systems is driven by the same atmospheric dynamics on both Mars and an Earth-like atmosphere, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. Furthermore, the findings provide valuable insights into the characteristics that an exoplanet's atmosphere must possess in order to support baroclinic storm formation, which is a crucial factor in determining the planet's habitability.

The Hankel path is a crucial component in complex analysis, enabling the representation of special functions like the Gamma function through contour integrals. A key aspect of this path is its interaction with vertical lines in the complex plane, specifically how it behaves when these lines intersect the path. A recent study by Parisi and his colleagues (2020) established conditions for the Hankel path to intersect vertical lines at points with known coordinates. Building on this research, our study explores how the Hankel path can be shaped to form a complex triangle with a vertical line, thereby enabling the representation of the double Gamma function as a contour integral. Additionally, we derive a closed-form expression for the function resulting from the product of two double Gamma functions, which is analogous to the classical Euler's beta function.

Quantum systems undergoing non-equilibrium processes exhibit intriguing correlations that are challenging to accurately simulate using traditional linearized hydrodynamic methods. To address this, we develop a new stochastic hydrodynamic scheme based on the linearized nonequilibrium quantum fluid dynamics, coupled with a corrected version of the Bogoliubov approximation for interacting Bose gases. This novel approach, which we call the 'deformed' BHE, offers a more precise simulation of non-equilibrium correlations by accounting for quantum fluctuations within the hydrodynamic framework. Through comprehensive numerical investigations, we demonstrate the BHE's ability to accurately capture correlation functions and observe a significant improvement over the traditional linearized approach. Moreover, we observe that the 'deformed' BHE consistently outperforms the BHE in multiple scenarios, validating its effectiveness in simulating non-equilibrium quantum correlations.

Neural backbone networks are widely used in computer vision tasks, with teachers typically being deeper and more complex than students. This depth discrepancy leads to a disconnect between the teacher's capability to learn and the student's limited capacity to learn it, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this issue, we propose the Hard Instance Normalization technique, which hardwires instance normalization layers in student networks, enabling them to mimic the behavior of deeper teacher networks. This normalized student network then learns to optimize the free parameters of instance normalization, achieving better performance with hard instance normalization than with regular instance normalization. Our method demonstrates excellent versatility, applicable to various Teacher-Student architectures, including convolutional and attention-based networks, and outperforms existing methods in multiple benchmark tests.

We introduce Bucket Elimination, a broad technique that incorporates inference and optimization tasks in graphical models. Our method expands on existing elimination strategies like clique elimination and joining elimination, and it also generalizes variable elimination approaches like Sum-Product and the inside-out method. The Bucket Elimination framework provides a unified framework for a variety of algorithms, enables the creation of customized algorithms based on specific situations, and offers a tool for analyzing the performance of variable elimination approaches.

We provide a detailed description of the centralizer $Z(n)_{sl2}$ within the $n$-th tensor power of the Lie algebra $sl2$, focusing on its component wise decomposition. This decomposition yields the centralizer's Hilbert-Poincar\'e series, which we then use to determine the number of linearly independent generators of $Z(n)_{sl2}$ for any positive integer $n$. Moreover, we derive an explicit formula to calculate the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer's component wise decomposition for any positive integer $i$ less than $n$, excluding cases where $i$ is a multiple of $4$ and $n$ is even.

This paper introduces an exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test, which is a non-parametric statistical test for evaluating the significance of within-participant correlations. The new algorithm builds upon the existing exact algorithm for simple-permutation tests and incorporates a new step to account for the paired nature of the test. The new algorithm's efficiency is measured in terms of computational time and memory usage in comparison to using Monte Carlo approximation. The results show that the new algorithm outperforms the existing algorithm for simple-permutation tests and offers significant gains when using the Monte Carlo approximation is not sufficient due to the large number of possible permutations.

Recent data from Pb-Pb collisions at LHC energies has revealed an intriguing pattern of dependence between the transverse momentum of triangular flow $v_3$ and elliptic flow $v_2$ for identified particles. Unlike the linear increase observed previously for $0.5 < p_T < 2$ GeV, recent findings show a slowing of the rise in the ratio of $v_3/v_2$ for larger transverse momenta. Further, recent data from p-Pb collisions at LHC energies has shown that the transverse momentum dependence of $v_3/v_2$ for identified particles behaves similarly to that in elliptical flow for hadrons. A single-scattering model, assuming anisotropic gluon distribution and weak coupling approximation, was utilized to analyze the ratio of $v_3/v_2$; this model predicts a linear increase in the ratio for transverse momenta less than 2 GeV. However, due to non-linear scattering effects, an abrupt decline in the ratio is anticipated at larger transverse momenta. The similarity between triangular and elliptical flow anisotropies for identified particles at transverse momenta greater than 2 GeV was found to be unaffected by initial state collisions; instead, it is likely a sign of a linear $p_T$ increase of anisotropy ratios $\epsilon_2$ and $\epsilon_3$ prior to scattering.

We develop a novel algorithm to track previously unseen targets with limited sensor fields of view, different from standard dynamic programming approaches. This algorithm, targeted at this specific tracking task, bypasses recalculation of the optimal policy at each time step, reducing complexity. More significantly, this algorithm allows for the integration of prior knowledge about target trajectories, enabling the creation of policies before sensor data is obtained. This is particularly beneficial in scenarios with sensor fields of view that are narrowly angled, such as with drones equipping cameras. By leveraging this algorithm, we can solve the problem of tracking previously unseen targets with limited sensor fields of view more efficiently, deviating from the standard dynamic programming method by orders of magnitude. On average, this algorithm is 100 times more efficient in computing the optimal policy than using standard dynamic programming, with some cases showing a complexity reduction of 10,000 times.

Building on the concept of an action-value function in decision-making theory, we've developed a novel way to evaluate actions in soccer based on their potential rewards. This approach allows for comparing the effectiveness of various actions, such as committing a foul or the ball going out of bounds, in relation to the potential of taking a shot on goal. Using this framework, we've designed two different strategies for choosing shots on goal, which serve as the foundation for creating shot-taking policies. To test these policies and evaluate their performance, we've created a simulator modeling a standard soccer game, taking into account factors such as team positions, the ball's movement, and time intervals. Through extensive simulations, we've determined the optimal shooting frequency in various scenarios, which can be used to inform player decisions on the field.

The integration of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) into various applications has grown significantly, leading to an increased demand for automated setup manipulation to expedite experimental procedures. In response to this need, we present a novel control system dubbed "LabCoach," which enables the automation of experimental setups incorporating MEMS devices, as well as their connection to telework platforms for remote access. This system leverages a multi-camera vision system to identify components, a 3D printer for creating custom fixtures, and a robotic arm for assembling the setup, allowing for the creation and modification of setups tailored to specific experiments. To demonstrate its effectiveness, LabCoach was used to automate an experiment for generating and analyzing nanomechanical resonators, which resulted in a significant reduction of setup preparation time and enabled the exploration of new experimental scenarios. The entire setup, including the robotic arm, vision system, and connectivity to telework platforms, can be easily managed and operated using a user-friendly interface available on desktop computers, tablets, or smartphones.

We investigate the stability of solitary waves in a nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with an anharmonic oscillator, focusing on the fundamental solitary wave as the initial condition. Unlike the harmonic oscillator, this system's nonlinear correction leads to a non-conserved energy framework, necessitating an approach that analyzes the stability based on the conserved quantities alone. By transitioning to a frame of reference moving at the solitary wave's speed, we establish a stability criterion utilizing the remaining conserved quantities. Specifically, we derive bounds on the wave's oscillations by mapping the problem to that of a classical anharmonic oscillator, whose oscillatory behavior is well-defined in specific parameter ranges. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of this criterion through numerical simulations, exploring how the presence of anharmonicity affects the stability of the solitary wave by adjusting key parameters.

Detecting infrequently decaying particles that linger briefly as they travel through a collider is a challenging task. A method that could help in searching for such particles, missing transom energy (MET), may not always be effective, and an alternative approach is to look for displaced vertices, which could indicate the particle's decay site. The choice between these methods depends on the particle's decay length, which is unpredictable for long-lived neutrals. However, their behavior can be understood through a novel perspective - how the particle's motion affects its probability of decaying near a vertex, which could be a collision point or a piece of the detector itself. To better comprehend this, consider a neutral particle that can take the form of a light beam as it travels; if it enters a region where it decays more frequently, it's equivalent to shining a brighter beam in that area. The region's shape reflects the particle's tendency to settle near vertices or move further, spreading out before decaying, which is analogous to the particle's ability to form bound states with other particles. The decay pattern of a neutral long-lived particle is thus comparable to the behavior of a light beam within a detector, which can be optimized by selecting the appropriate search strategy between MET and displaced vertex analysis.

This research focuses on understanding how language models respond to
semantically altered words and contexts. We develop a method to analyze
changes in contextual variance and demonstrate how it influences the
models' ability to detect subtle word meanings. Using this approach, we
investigate how contextual variance impacts the performance of both
regular and embedding-based features in language models. Our findings
reveal that slight contextual variations can significantly alter the
interpretation of word meanings and may even lead to the activation of
latent word meanings not present in the original context. We also use
this method to analyze the effects of contextual variance on the
distribution of contextual features and the resulting semantic shifts.
Furthermore, we utilize a dataset containing context-dependent words
to evaluate the efficacy of both regular and embedding-based features
in capturing context-dependent word meanings. Our results indicate that
Contextualized Embeddings outperform both Sloan's (Sloan 1993) and
Keller's (Keller 1977) models in describing the variability of word
meanings and their relationships.

Our research involved analyzing observations from 25 years of AXION-LC proposed particle collider data, which was simulated as part of a technical design report. We examined the connection between dark minispaces involving ultra-light bosonic particles and the proposed detector's capability to detect dark matter particles, Axions or ALP's, through their interaction with atomic nuclei. The research focused on a specific type of dark minospaces, represented by a three-dimensional grid with 10x10x10 unit cells, and the corresponding dark matter particle properties. The results revealed that the proposed detector would be ineffective in detecting dark minospaces consisting of ultra-light bosonic particles as it wouldn't be able to capture sufficient dark matter particle anomalies. This inadequacy could potentially impact the contribution of certain types of dark matter to overall dark matter composition.

Quantum systems subjected to continuous driving are investigated here, focusing on the role of coherent states within these systems. A novel, intuitive picture is presented, demonstrating how coherent states serve as the fundamental building blocks for describing the behavior of driven quantum systems. Through this framework, the dynamics of such systems can be accurately predicted and understood, offering a distinct perspective on quantum interference phenomena and their control. Furthermore, this description enables the straightforward identification of the generated correlations within coupled systems, providing a clear view of the mechanisms behind non-trivial quantum states formation, including entanglement and even complex patterns of entanglement.

We have developed a quantum relational Hoare logic that enables us to write specifications detailing the connection between a program's inputs and outputs, and to verify that programs meet these specifications. This logic can be used to write specifications that describe the relationship between particular input values and output values, as well as guidelines for linking inputs and outputs more generally, in a manner that is proportional to the program's output, rather than being limited to fixed values. This is similar to how we describe the relationship between inputs and outputs in classical logic, but with an important difference, as in quantum mechanics, observing the relationship between two variables can affect their actual connection.

This paper presents a novel approach to accurately determining magnetic fields within vector magnetic field maps, particularly in areas with complex structure and strong field strengths. The method involves accounting for the fraction of the pixel occupied by magnetic features, which is particularly effective in capturing the behavior of arcsec-resolution maps like those obtained through local helioseismology. By explicitly considering this fill fraction in the calculation, we can significantly improve the accuracy of vector magnetic field assessments, especially in regions with strong field strengths and in patches with overlapping features. A key aspect of this approach is the use of a non-linear effect to analyze the impact of fill fraction on magnetic field measurements. We apply this technique to a model magnetogram to demonstrate its accuracy and validity before applying it to an actual local helioseismology vector magnetic field map. The results show that the fill fraction method offers a number of benefits over traditional methods, including reduced error and better reflection of true magnetic field behavior.

Building upon the theory of geodesics in Coxeter groups, we explore a specific type of geodesic called a wedge, which is defined as a sequence of spheres centered around the identity element in a hyperbolic space of dimension at least 2. A key component of this study is the number of spheres within a wedge of a given size, which is shown to be directly connected to the size of a generating set in the Coxeter group. More specifically, we establish that the number of spheres in a wedge is proportional to the square of the minimum size of a generating set, allowing for some adjustment to account for non-simple geodesics. Additionally, we develop a straightforward method for calculating the number of spheres based on the structure of the generating set, which involves pairs of generating elements that fail to satisfy certain conditions.

This research paper confirms that certain curves, specifically those in Euclidean spaces of two and three dimensions, do not conform to the standards of Blaschke curves, due to failing to meet the requirements of being a Bertrand curve.

Recently, there has been a surge in research using information-theoretic loss functions like KL Divergence and Jensen-Shannon Divergence. Despite under-performance in some tasks, these loss functions have shown potential and are being explored for various applications. This paper investigates why under-represented loss functions might yield inferior performance compared to more established choices like mean squared error. To address this, we develop a novel loss function called the Generalized Jensen-Shannon Divergence Loss, which builds on JS D. By applying information-theoretic loss functions through regularization, we can evaluate their performance and and establish a theoretical framework to compare them with each other and other loss functions. Moreover, we propose a novel optimization algorithm called Informed Policy Iteration, which is capable of optimizing under-represented loss functions without compromising convergence. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that information-theoretic loss functions can be effective options, with the GJSD loss outperforming other choices in multiple tasks.

Neural models have excelled in natural language processing tasks but require substantial domain-specific data. We propose a method called Relation-Type Aware (RTA) where neural models are trained on the hierarchy of if-then relation types. This hierarchy allows for more effective organization of relation-type datasets and reduces data dissemination costs. Our experiments using BERT and RoBERTa base models on OBOWD's if-then relation dataset showed that RTA outperformed the regular training approach for all three tasks: classification, generation, and convolutional encoding. Notably, RTA achieved the best results across the board with BERT, demonstrating its potential by reducing relation-type datasets to just two categories. Our findings suggest that neural models can benefit from a more comprehensive hierarchy of relation-types and may even learn from it without explicit labeling.

If a video shows novel viewpoints, it is challenging to predict its corresponding image. Recently, a method called ViewTransformer was developed, which utilizes a dual representation of videos consisting of both the current and predicted images. This dual representation allows for the effective use of attention mechanisms to forecast novel viewpoint images. Unlike traditional image generation models, ViewTransformer generates videos by transforming the representation of the current image. This transformation process involves a multi-step approach using multiple predicted images, which are then combined to achieve the desired viewpoint. Furthermore, the method incorporates a novel perspective-based loss function to guarantee the generated images are aesthetically pleasing and realistic. Evaluations using multiple datasets including Horizon, Relighting, and DTI showed that ViewTransformer outperforms existing approaches in predicting novel viewpoint images.

We provide a detailed examination of how truncating the geodesic distance in a graph based on a specified threshold value affects its metric dimension. It is demonstrated that maximizing this truncated dimension results in the same minimum number of nodes required for representation as does maximizing the original geodesic distance. Additionally, we identify a polynomial-time algorithm to compute the truncated metric dimension by alternatingly updating and evaluating the possible minimum representations, which takes O(n^4 \cdot 2^n) time, where n represents the graph's node count.

We develop a noise-reducing framework called NSE-RNE to address cardiac condition detection issues resulting from electrical noise. This framework combines a noise-reduced signal component with a model that forecasts on missing data, addressing the challenge of distinguishing noisy signals. We introduce a deep learning model called RHA-CNN, consisting of a residual attention block with a convolutional neural network, designed to filter out noise and enhance signal quality. This RHA-CNN model is particularly effective for detecting conditions like cardiac arrhythmias that present as minor signal variations. To further improve condition detection, we use a feature extraction technique called PCA, which helps identify the most distinct characteristics of signal patterns. This technique is particularly valuable for distinguishing between similar patterns such as normal and abnormal heart rhythms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NSE-RNE in noise-introduced datasets and its potential to be applied across various heart signal sensors and devices.

We discovered two types of physical connections between starburst galaxies and their surroundings through our observations of CI line emissions and massive halo reservoirs. The ratio of [CII]12-1 to far-infrared dust emission is known to be influenced by the presence of low-density molecular winds or CGM reservoirs around these galaxies. By analyzing data from the ALMA and HST, we found that the ratio of CI line emissions to far-infrared dust emission is also affected in a similar way, indicating that CI lines reflect the extension of starburst galaxies into their surroundings. This conclusion is supported by the similar shapes of molecular gas reservoirs detected through CI and [CII] lines, as well as the similar environments they occupy, which are characterized by low densities of a few times 10^-5 cm^-3.

We establish explicit, simple formulas to calculate the velocity distribution of a second-class particle in ASEP (Artificial Spin Ice) over time, without relying on partial differential equations. These formulas are derived through combinatorial methods, specifically by utilizing the lattice path model's connection to ASEP and the definition of ballot numbers.

As contact tracing processes evolve, understanding the dynamics of infectious disease spread becomes increasingly complex. Postulating that infected individuals come into contact with a random set of peers is one common approach to modeling this phenomenon, although it may not accurately reflect real-world tracing efforts. This research takes a novel approach by treating traced contacts as a finite resource that is distributed and utilized differently among various age groups. To quantify the impact of this resource allocation on disease spread, this study fits and compares differential equation models to real outbreak data from Myanmar (2021) and Oklahoma (2019). By analyzing and contrasting these models, this study demonstrates that the effectiveness of contact tracing can significantly influence the rate of disease spread and ultimately the duration of outbreaks.

Observations from the GALEX over a vast area of 700 square degrees have been combined with data from the SDSS to examine the relationship between NUV-r color and galaxy mass. Contrary to expectations, a positive correlation was found for low-mass galaxies. However, a striking reversal in this correlation was observed once a mass threshold of approximately $10^{10.2}M_{\odot}$ is exceeded. Beyond this point, more massive galaxies show a decreased NUV-r color, indicating bluer NUV-r values for them compared to their lower-mass counterparts. This reversal in correlation is particularly evident when considering narrow mass ranges ($<0.2dex$ apart) and appears to be unaffected by the type of galaxy (E/S0 versus spiral) or redshift. A model was also developed to simulate the behavior of galaxies based on their mass, and results from this model closely mimic the observed correlation trends.

Multilingual language models have excelled in predicting the sentiment of English texts, but struggle with texts in other languages, particularly those with limited training data. To address this, we propose Multitask Adaptation for BERT (MAB), a framework that enables such models to classify sentiments in non-English texts. Our approach involves modifying the existing sentiment classification task to account for language differences, by using a multilingual corpus and adding a language identification layer to the task. We conducted experiments using three non-English languages (French, German, and Italian) and achieved impressive results, outperforming previous studies. Our results demonstrate that MAB can effectively adapt to new languages with limited training data, and recommends a data preparation procedure to aid in training these models.

We observed an unusual rotation profile in KIC 9267654, a star that shows chromospheric activity indicating it's a young object, but with a slow rotational speed of about 13 days. To better understand this profile, we analyzed the star's achromatic signal variation and its chromospheric indicator, and applied various tests to rule out biases and inconsistencies. The data from Keplercame from two consecutive years, allowing us to investigate the profile's symmetry and possible causes of its unusual shape. We considered several scenarios, including the star's true rotation period being significantly longer than 13 days, differential rotation, spectroscopic binary status, eclipse patterns, stellar convection patterns, magnetic field behavior, and the presence of a stellar companion. To confirm our findings, we analyzed another similar star, KIC 11700025, which showed a similar unusual rotation profile.

Fake news on social media has become a pressing concern, and automated systems are being developed to help detect it. The MetaFEND system is a machine learning-based system intended to detect false information spread through media. This project extends the MetaFEND system to recognize false information about impending global events, which can be challenging to identify with standard techniques. A key improvement to the MetaFEND system is a new module called MetaFEND-N, which utilizes natural language processing tools to search multiple sources of information more effectively. This research also includes two novel datasets, GlobEvent and GlobEvent-K, consisting of information both true and false regarding global events. The dataset GlobEvent-K is further sub-classified into three categories of events: conflicts, natural disasters, and economic events. The MetaFEND-N system has been tested on both datasets, demonstrating its capability to detect false information with higher accuracy than traditional methods. The data collected during this project has been made available to the public for use in future research.

A Golay complementary array pair is defined as two quaternary arrays, G0 and G1, of order p, where their differences have exactly one or zero. To determine the feasibility of a quaternary Golay complementary array pair, we propose two constructions based on the idea of coloring graphs and the concept of semi-partially balanced codes. The first construction involves coloring graphs with specific properties, and the second involves coloring graphs that have loops and multi-edges. We also investigate the feasible sizes of such pairs by analyzing possible values of p modulo various integers. Moreover, we provide a summary of previously known feasible sizes and their combinations to outline the condition that such sizes must satisfy.

This study develops a novel method called Siren-UNet, which utilizes a neural network to accurately segment regions of interest in medical images. Leveraging a UNet structure and Siren, a neural network that can learn implicit representations of data through self-attractive connections, Siren-UNet aims to bypass the need for convolutional operations and their associated computational costs. Instead, the network can focus on learning complex segmentation patterns and adjusts the implicit representation of the image to fit the segmentation task. To further enhance the segmentation outcome, Siren-UNET includes an additional neural network to account for boundary information of the ROI. Through extensive experiments on publicly available datasets, the Siren-UNET approach demonstrates remarkable segmentation performance and outshines state-of-the-art methods by achieving significant time savings and improved segmentation accuracy.

This paper introduces a novel, joint optimization framework for both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction, called the Regularized Block-Dynamic Multi-Task Learning approach. The framework is designed to simultaneously solve multiple supervised classification tasks and unsupervised clustering tasks, allowing for variable numbers of features to be effective. The framework's key characteristic is the utilization of block-diagonal structures to efficiently manage feature extraction for different tasks, which results in substantially reduced dimensionality. The approach is highly efficient, able to adapt to situations where the number of data points is small, by using a regularized version of the block-dynamic multi-task learning model. Notably, the framework can be used for both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction, eliminating the need for task-specific protocols, which is a major innovation.

Recent advances in question-answering models have shown promising results, particularly those pre-trained on knowledge graphs consisting of factual triples. These models have an advantage over traditionally text-based pre-trained models, as they can directly learn relationships and information linking concepts. Despite this potential benefit, research has shown that KG-pretrained models often struggle with questions that require concept categorization. This pattern holds true even when comparing the performance of models pre-trained on knowledge graphs to those trained on conventional text data. To address this disparity, this study introduces a novel training approach called Triple-E, which focuses on triple-based embeddings and combines them with category information. This method enables the model to better grasp concept hierarchies and allows for efficient learning of new categories. The results of various question-answering tasks demonstrate that KG-pretrained models perform consistently better when employing the Triple-E approach, and in some cases, outperform conventionally text-based pre-trained models.

The non-linear Yang-Mills charge within the context of an electromagnetic field is investigated for astrophysical black holes. A generalization of the charge parameter is employed to analyze how it affects the shadow radius and the thermal profile of these black holes. The shadow radius of the charge-black hole is found to increase with the non-linear Yang-Mills charge, with its influence depending on the type of non-linearity. The FPE (Fierz-Pauli-Einstein) and power-law non-linearities exhibit similar trends, whereas a harmonic non-linearity shows a divergent shadow radius for specific conditions. The shadow radius's behavior in the presence of a external electromagnetic field is also examined, which shows that the field's strength can amplify the effect of the non-linear charge on the shadow radius. The thermal profile of the non-linear charged black hole is found to vary significantly with the charge parameter, with its influence depending on the type of non-linearity. The FPE non-linearity results in a thermal profile that exhibits a peak-value reduction, whereas a harmonic non-linearity leads to an increased peak-value. The external electromagnetic field's strength is found to amplify the thermal profile's variation in the presence of non-linear charges.

We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the influence of non-classical phenomena, specifically entanglement and intangibility, on the shape of an optical tomogram. Our approach involves a combination of the Schmidt decomposition and an analysis of marginal distributions. Through this method, we determine the conditions under which non-classical behavior appears in the optical tomogram of a two-partite system after the parts have been separated by an unknown SU(2)-invariant interaction. Additionally, we explore how entanglement change affects the tomographic image without directly observing the non-classical effect. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between non-classical behavior in the optical tomogram and the Wigner function of the system.

The paper reports the results of a statistical analysis targeting specific decay modes of beauty mesons. This analysis was conducted using a 2.0 ab^-1 data set of proton-proton collisions collected by the CERN LHC from 2015-2018, corresponding to 1.7 ab^-1 of 13-TeV data and 0.3 ab^-1 of 8-TeV data. The decay modes of interest include B_s^0 to D_s^- K+, B_s^0 to D_s^- pi+, B_s^0 to mu^- bar mu+, B_s^0 to tau^- bar tau+, B^0 to D^- pi+, B^0 to D^- K^+, B^0 to mu^- bar mu+, and B^0 to tau^- bar tau+. The branching fractions of these decay modes were determined, with some representing the most precise measurements to date.

We prove that for modules with minimal non-trivial sublattice reconstruction, their composition factor decomposition mirrors their underlying module structure. This involves a deep examination of their submodule lattices and the relationship with their composition factor decomposition.

We provide a detailed examination of how biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space are related to values of certain recurrent operators. Specifically, we derive novel conditions for biharmonic hypersurfaces to be minimal, as well as additional information on their geometric properties. We demonstrate that our findings offer improved standards compared to previously established standards.

We establish a characterization for p/q-recognisable subsets of the set (N_p/q)^d by showing that such subsets are equivalent to subsets defined by rational expressions over the set (N_p/q)^d, and we also establish the equivalence with first-order logic over the structure (N_p/q,+,x^), sharing constant symbols from (N_p/q)^d.

We examine the underlying dynamics of pseudoscalar meson decay modes through the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed expansion frameworks. A key distinction between these frameworks lies in their approach to describing decay rates, with the former using a effective field theory model and the latter relying on a QCD-based approach. To bridge the gap between these frameworks, we recast the BGL expansion to mirror the effective description used in CLN, focusing on the role of anomalous chromoelectric dipole moments in their comparison. Through this adjustment, we find that the CLN and BGL frameworks yield comparable descriptions of near-threshold decay patterns, with the BGL framework offering additional insights into the underlying physics.

This study focuses on the development of a novel, efficient method for calculating
Lyapunov exponents, particularly in complex dynamical systems, as well as its initial
application to a specific scenario. The linearized, linear time-evolving reference system
plays a crucial role in determining the first Lyapunov exponent of a given dynamical system.
The method involves using the distance evolution between the linearized reference systems
around the trajectory of the original system to calculate the exponent. By interpreting the
exponent as an indicator of stability, we demonstrated the translational stability of a
conservative, driven XY model in a square lattice, as well as its conservation of energy.
Furthermore, we observed the system's temperature fluctuations through the exponent's
behavior. The results were also verified through numerical simulations of the same system
using the initial conditions of Arnoux-Yor and Kruzhkov's techniques.

Researchers in the field of geometric analysis have extended the concept of an angle function to Riemannian manifolds with positive curvature, specifically to spaces of constant positive curvature and spherical products. Building on this, the current study introduces the condition of global conformal hyperbolicity in certain Riemannian spaces, then uses this condition to solve problems related to conformal embeddability in these spaces. Specifically, the study establishes the relationship between the degree of a mapping and the size of its interface, as well as the connection between injective conformal embeddings and the embedding problem in spherical products.

We have developed a new framework called TPC, which is the first to achieve certified accuracy under a wide range of twisting transformations in point cloud models. Our TPC framework is grounded in geometric deep learning fundamentals, specifically the initial work by Bruna et al. and the more recent reformulation by Hermant et al. Our first significant finding is that Bruna's original definition requires significant modification to function properly under twisting transformations. Our second significant finding involves demonstrating that Bruna's original definition necessitates substantial revision to ensure it operates effectively under twisting transformations. To reestablish Bruna's original definition, we created a new description called description C, which serves as the foundation for our TPC framework. Our key contribution involves designing a new framework called TPC, which is the first to achieve certified accuracy under a wide range of twisting transformations in point cloud models. Our TPC framework is based on a novel description called description C, which differs from the traditional description A used in Bruna's original definition. Our findings demonstrate that Bruna's original definition is equivalent to description C, confirming our reformation is valid.
